summary: An eval case can now be built from what Nora ACTUALLY knew about a real room at a real past moment, instead of from invented dialogue: nora.subject.sandbox.sandbox_from_snapshot() reads a historical snapshot and copies it into an isolated eval subject.
details: nora/subject/sandbox.py: sandbox_from_snapshot(subject, platform=, conversation_id=, before_ms=, culture_key=, unit=) reads the real room once through nora.infra.sql.snapshot.snapshot() -- which carries no INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE and so cannot write -- and seeds the reconstruction into the room and workspace obtain() already isolated. It takes no write target: the entry point driven afterwards may write a note, a reminder or a reply, and every one of those has to land in the copy.

The clock is SHIFTED, not copied. Every timestamp moves by now_ms - before_ms, and the standing's staleness is measured against before_ms, so a row that was ten minutes old at the instant is ten minutes old in the sandbox. Copying ts verbatim is faithful to the database and wrong for the model: ages are what reach it, so a snapshot of last July would render as a room that had said nothing for two months.

Real account ids do not travel. Message has no sender_id field, so _speakers() mints synthetic ones; person_id IS copied, because it is an identity.toml handle rather than an account. Pinned against the messages.sender_id column, not against the dataclass.

Knowledge gains a `culture` field -- one account body, written through SqlCultureStore.append (production's own write lane, which moves the head in the same transaction) keyed on the room's conversation_id, which build_config now guarantees equals the room's resolved primary_id (see the fourth-pass fix below) rather than merely by convention. It is one body rather than a chain because CultureAdaptor.inputs renders head.body and nothing else, so a case stating a chain would be stating input no entry point can observe.
Message.name widened to str | None, because messages.sender_name is nullable and a sealed-sender row has no display name -- mapping one onto "Unknown" would invent a name the room never saw.
Not wired into evals/corpora or the eval CLI: this is the capability only.

Found by independent verification, across two passes, and fixed before merge -- both times a refusal keyed on the wrong identifier for one of the writes know() makes, both times reproduced live against Postgres before the fix: (1) the original self-seed refusal (platform, conversation_id) == subject.room did not cover culture (keyed on conversation_id alone -- primary_id has no platform component) or notes (keyed on memory.workspace_id, not subject.room at all), so a cross-platform pair sharing a conversation_id, or a unit left at the subject's own workspace default, reached the real room's culture chain or notebook; (2) fixing (1) by widening the room check still left the transcript itself exposed, because SqlRecordStore's reads (recent/since/since_including_nora) filter on conversation_id ALONE -- TranscriptRow carries no platform column -- so a cross-platform, same-conversation_id pair still passed the tuple check and its clock-shifted rows (sorted NEWEST) came back out of the real room's own recent(). The room/transcript check is now keyed on conversation_id alone, matching the read path it guards; the culture and unit checks are unchanged and are not redundant with it, since culture_key and unit are independent of conversation_id by design.

A THIRD pass found a deeper gap in a pre-existing function, nora/subject/obtain.py's default_policy() -- not fixable by adding a fourth refusal, because the problem was not a missing check but two composed values silently disagreeing. A subject built with a memory.workspace_id override and no explicit policy got a generated policy.toml with no unit key, so Conversation.unit fell back to its own shipped default ("nora") regardless of the override. Production resolves EVERY unit-keyed read -- notes, via nora.app.composition._note_unit_of, the <notes> prompt block -- through Conversation.unit, never through memory.workspace_id, so this meant seeded notes could be invisible to the very turn the sandbox exists to drive, or (whenever a real deployment's own unit happened to be left at its shipped default too) a live turn's note write landing in real production data with none of the three isolation refusals able to see it, because none of them compares the value production actually reads. Fixed by having default_policy() take the resolved unit and build_config() pass memory.workspace_id's resolved value through.

A FOURTH pass found the third pass's own fix covered only the branch where build_config generates the policy -- an explicit spec.policy (which every ported corpus case states) went through an unchanged check that was a SUBSTRING test over the raw TOML text (f'id = "{room[1]}"' in policy), not a resolution. Reproduced live, three ways: an explicit policy whose unit disagreed with memory.workspace_id composed cleanly (the exact defect the third pass fixed, reached through the untouched branch); a multi-entry policy where the room's id string sat on a DIFFERENT entry composed cleanly with primary_id resolving to a real OTHER room, so culture/notes/the Dreamer's scope would key under that room's identifiers instead of the subject's own; a policy whose only entry was on a different PLATFORM than the subject's room (the substring check cannot see platform at all) composed cleanly with the room resolving to nothing, so ingest would refuse every message with nothing raising. Fixed at the root, replacing the substring test entirely: build_config now reads back the policy.toml it just wrote through the real parser (nora.policy.load_policy) and refuses unless the resolved Conversation both names the subject's own room as its primary_id AND carries the resolved unit -- whichever branch produced the policy. Two pre-existing, now-corrected comments (nora/subject/knowledge.py, this branch's own integration test) had asserted the substring check as a soundness guarantee; both now describe the actual, resolved one.

A FIFTH pass found the fourth pass's own unit check was grounded on a value RE-DERIVED from spec.overrides (with its own hardcoded "nora" fallback), not on cfg.memory.workspace_id -- the value know() actually writes notes under. For a subject with no memory.workspace_id override, agreement rested on three literals in three files (config.example.toml, nora/policy.py, obtain.py) happening to coincide -- not live today, since the shipped template does say "nora", but the same convention-not-construction shape the whole fix exists to close, one layer further down. Fixed by reordering build_config: config.toml is now loaded and overridden BEFORE the policy is written, so the unit check (and default_policy()'s own default, when no explicit policy is stated) is grounded on the actually-composed cfg.memory.workspace_id, not a guess. Reproduced live by shipping a template whose own default workspace_id diverged from "nora"; the old check passed it, the new one grounds on the real value regardless of what any file's default happens to say. A caller overriding policy_file to point the composed config at a policy build_config did not write is a known, remaining theoretical gap -- no caller does this anywhere in this repo today, and closing it is a second, separable change (resolving through cfg.policy_file rather than the fixed spec.workdir/policy.toml path).
limitations: Media is not reconstructed. The snapshot returns messages.body as stored, which carries a handle ([image a3f2c1]) rather than a description; synthesising a MediaBlob here would give the handle a digest that names a different blob, so seeded rows show bare handles.

Reply threading is flattened. snapshot.py's quoted_ts names which earlier row a message replied to; Message has no quote field, so as_knowledge drops it, and nora.agent.prefill's reply lines never render for a copied room. Closing it needs a citation-style id translation, not a field, so it is left open rather than fixed here.

A note anchored only by entity ids is refused by name rather than seeded: NoteSeed can state an anchor_date and not an entity list, and such a note would otherwise reach Note.__post_init__ with no anchor at all.

The read and the write share one physical database -- cases are isolated by room and workspace naming, not by a database each -- so pointing this at real history means the synthetic copy is written into the same Postgres the history lives in.

build_config's resolved-policy check reads back spec.workdir/policy.toml, not cfg.policy_file -- a caller overriding policy_file to point production at a different file would bypass the check entirely. No caller does this anywhere in this repo; closing it is a separable follow-up.

Isolation is a Postgres-only guarantee. Every tool this branch's own isolation checks cover (notes, reminders/events, the transcript, culture) is keyed in the SAME physical database sandbox_from_snapshot writes into, which is what makes room/unit isolation possible at all. Two classes of tool sit entirely outside that boundary and read or write LIVE, unfrozen, real-world state regardless of which room or unit the driven turn is composed against: (1) Honcho-backed tools -- ask_memory, remember, search_memory, search_memory_workspace -- keyed on the real person_id the snapshot faithfully copies (by design, so a case can cite who said something), so remember writes a real conclusion about a real person and ask_memory reads today's memory of them, not the reconstructed instant's; (2) presence/Life360-backed tools -- where_is, where_been, saved_places -- which force a fresh live location read on every call, entirely independent of before_ms. Neither is a defect this branch introduces or one a Postgres-side fix can close: closing it would mean giving Honcho and presence their own isolated/frozen identity for an eval run, which is a separate, undecided design question. A corpus case built from a real snapshot that drives an entry point capable of reaching either tool class is not fully reproducible and can read or write real personal data; this is the concrete risk to weigh when choosing which historical scenarios to wire up next.
